clinicalPearls: MRI is generally more sensitive than CT for lesions of the central and peripheral nervous system, whereas CT is faster and the pragmatic first choice for uncooperative patients and for suspected acute stroke, hemorrhage, or acute intracranial/spinal trauma (Harrison 22e p.3383).

Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the single most sensitive technique for detecting acute cerebral or spinal cord ischemia, with restricted diffusion (high DWI signal) appearing in infarction of less than about 7 days; it also lights up encephalitis, abscess, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (Harrison 22e p.3383, 3389).

CT is superior to MRI for fine osseous detail and is preferred for the initial workup of conductive hearing loss and skull/spine bone lesions, while MRI better detects bone-marrow infiltrative processes that CT may miss (Harrison 22e p.3383).

On unenhanced CT, denser structures such as bone or acute blood appear bright (high attenuation), whereas water, air, and soft tissue appear dark; this is why acute hemorrhage and bone are well seen on noncontrast CT (Harrison 22e p.3383-3384).

Iodinated contrast highlights vascular structures and blood-brain barrier defects; in the normal CNS only vessels and structures lacking a blood-brain barrier (pituitary, choroid plexus, dura) enhance (Harrison 22e p.3384).

Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is highly sensitive to blood, calcium, and air and is the sequence of choice for microhemorrhages seen in amyloid angiopathy, hypertension, hemorrhagic metastases, traumatic brain injury, and thrombotic states (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388).

FLAIR suppresses the bright CSF signal of T2 imaging, improving detection of edematous/water-containing lesions adjacent to CSF spaces such as periventricular plaques and cortical lesions (Harrison 22e p.3387).

Gadolinium-based contrast does not cause contrast-induced nephropathy, but linear (group 1/3) agents can cause nephrogenic systemic fibrosis in patients with severe renal impairment; macrocyclic (group 2) agents are far safer and preferred in at-risk patients (Harrison 22e p.3388-3389).

Perfusion imaging that shows a region of prolonged mean transit time with preserved cerebral blood volume identifies tissue at risk (ischemic penumbra) that may be salvageable, distinct from infarcted core where blood volume and flow are reduced (Harrison 22e p.3390).
CTA and gadolinium-enhanced MRA have largely replaced catheter angiography, which is now reserved for cases needing fine small-vessel detail or planned interventional therapy (Harrison 22e p.3383).

Vessel wall MR imaging is a high-resolution technique that interrogates the arterial wall itself and helps distinguish atherosclerosis, primary CNS vasculitis, and reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome (Harrison 22e p.3390).

Amyloid PET can be positive in up to about 25% of cognitively normal older adults, so a positive scan does not by itself diagnose Alzheimer disease; tau PET appears more specific (Harrison 22e p.3392).
harrison.pathophysiology: Neuroimaging techniques exploit differing physical tissue properties. CT reconstructs a cross-sectional map of x-ray attenuation: dense tissue (bone, acute clot) attenuates heavily and appears bright, while water and air appear dark. MRI maps the distribution and relaxation behavior of (mainly hydrogen) protons placed in a strong static magnetic field and excited by radiofrequency pulses; T1 relaxation is the time for ~63% of protons to return toward equilibrium and T2 the time for ~63% to dephase. Manipulating pulse timing (TR and TE) yields T1-weighted images (fat and subacute hemorrhage bright; CSF/edema dark) or T2-weighted images (CSF/edema/demyelination/infarct bright). Gray matter contains roughly 10-15% more water than white matter, providing intrinsic contrast. Pathology such as infarction, abscess, and dense tumor restricts microscopic water motion, producing high DWI signal. Iodinated and gadolinium contrast agents reveal blood-brain barrier breakdown by tumor, infarct, or infection. Flow phenomena underlie MR angiography, and regional changes in oxy/deoxyhemoglobin underlie the BOLD signal of functional MRI (Harrison 22e p.3383-3392).
additionalDifferentials: Ring-enhancing lesion: cerebral abscess versus high-grade glioma or metastasis (restricted central diffusion favors abscess)
Restricted diffusion in medial temporal lobe: herpes simplex encephalitis versus acute infarction versus other limbic inflammatory processes
Multiple low-signal SWI foci: cerebral amyloid angiopathy versus chronic hypertensive microbleeds versus hemorrhagic metastases versus diffuse axonal injury
Focal arterial narrowing/wall enhancement: atherosclerosis versus primary CNS vasculitis versus reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Noncontrast CT for acute hemorrhage, trauma, and acute mental-status change
MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging for suspected ischemia, encephalitis, or abscess
CT angiography or gadolinium-enhanced/time-of-flight MR angiography for vascular assessment
Vessel wall MR imaging to characterize arteriopathies and vasculitis
Perfusion CT or perfusion MRI/ASL to assess core versus penumbra and tumor vascularity
CT myelography for failed-back syndrome, CSF fistula localization, and meningeal/arachnoid cysts
FDG-PET and amyloid/tau PET ligands for oncologic staging and neurodegenerative evaluation
Estimated GFR before contrast in at-risk patients
redFlags: Acute change in mental status, new focal deficit, or head/spine trauma warranting urgent noncontrast CT
Suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (CT then CTA, with lumbar puncture if CT negative)
Severe renal impairment (eGFR <30 mL/min per 1.73 m2) or dialysis raising concern for nephrogenic systemic fibrosis with linear gadolinium agents
Prior severe contrast (anaphylactoid) reaction, with eightfold higher recurrence risk for gadolinium
Ferromagnetic implants (some aneurysm clips, non-conditional pacemakers/defibrillators) or ocular metallic foreign body before MRI
Suspected spinal block or elevated intracranial pressure before myelography/lumbar puncture
harrison.prognosis: As a diagnostic modality, neuroimaging itself is generally safe. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury from iodinated contrast is rare, usually transient with creatinine returning toward baseline within 1-2 weeks, and most strongly associated with preexisting severe renal insufficiency; gadolinium does not cause it. Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis from linear gadolinium agents in severe renal failure is rare (reported incidence ~0.19-4% in GFR <30) but can be severely disabling with multiorgan fibrosis. Severe allergic reactions are uncommon (~0.04% with nonionic iodinated agents; gadolinium severe reactions exceedingly rare). Radiation-induced malignancy from diagnostic CT is felt to be minimal but is dose-dependent (Harrison 22e p.3384-3389).
pitfalls: Reliance on shellfish or iodine allergy to predict contrast reactions is unreliable; the strongest predictor is a prior contrast reaction (about fivefold risk), plus atopy/asthma and other drug/food allergies (Harrison 22e p.3385).
Premedication regimens shorter than 4-5 hours have no demonstrated efficacy and do not guarantee prevention of contrast reactions (Harrison 22e p.3387).
Bicarbonate and acetylcysteine have not shown protection over normal saline against contrast-associated AKI in recent meta-analyses (Harrison 22e p.3385).

MRA has lower spatial resolution than catheter angiography, is insensitive to slow flow, and may not distinguish near-complete from complete occlusion or detect small-vessel vasculitis/distal vasospasm (Harrison 22e p.3390).

Brain gadolinium deposition (dentate nuclei, globus pallidus) occurs even with normal renal/hepatic function, is dose-dependent and greater with linear agents, but to date has no proven neurotoxic histologic correlate (Harrison 22e p.3387-3388).
The MR magnet is always on; ferromagnetic missile injuries and torqued implants can be fatal, so rigorous screening of patients and staff is mandatory (Harrison 22e p.3389).
Patient motion degrades MRI; uncooperative patients should be sedated or imaged with CT, and children under ~8 years often require monitored anesthesia (Harrison 22e p.3389).
Iodinated contrast should be avoided before planned radioactive iodine thyroid therapy because it reduces radioisotope uptake (Harrison 22e p.3387).
harrison.severityClassification: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury is defined per KDIGO criteria within 48 h of contrast: absolute serum creatinine rise >=0.3 mg/dL (>26.4 micromol/L), a >=50% (>=1.5-fold) increase over baseline, or urine output <=0.5 mL/kg per h for at least 6 h. Renal-risk stratification for contrast uses eGFR, with <30 mL/min per 1.73 m2 carrying the greatest evidence for risk (normal >=90 mL/min per 1.73 m2) (Harrison 22e p.3384-3386).
management: Select noncontrast CT as the rapid first-line study for suspected acute haemorrhage, trauma or acute change in consciousness
Use MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging as the most sensitive test for acute ischaemia and for suspected encephalitis, abscess or demyelination
Choose CT or MR angiography and venography to assess arterial occlusion, aneurysm or cerebral venous thrombosis, and perfusion imaging to distinguish infarct core from salvageable penumbra
Screen for MRI safety contraindications such as implanted devices or metallic foreign bodies before scanning

Minimise contrast-associated risk by assessing renal function before iodinated or gadolinium contrast, hydrating at-risk patients, and avoiding less stable gadolinium agents in severe renal impairment to prevent nephrogenic systemic fibrosis
Limit ionising radiation through justified requesting and dose optimisation, particularly in children and pregnancy
Correlate imaging with the clinical question and involve neuroradiology to guide sequence selection and interpretation
